Italian Bank Workers Launch Nationwide Strike, Disrupting Branches and Digital Services

Banking operations across Italy faced severe disruption on Tuesday as thousands of employees staged a coordinated walkout over stalled contract negotiations and concerns about job security. The strike, organized by the National Union of Banking Employees (NUBE), began at 8 a.m. and is expected to continue for at least 48 hours, with the possibility of further action if talks with employers fail to progress.

The strike has affected major institutions including Credito Nuovo, Banca Italiana di Sviluppo, and Finanza Popolare, with over 60% of branch locations reportedly closed or operating with limited staff, according to union estimates. Digital banking platforms and call centers have also experienced delays, as many IT and customer service employees joined the industrial action.

Customers arriving at branch offices in Rome, Milan, and Naples encountered locked doors and posted notices explaining the walkout. “We understand the inconvenience this causes, but our members are determined to defend their rights,” said NUBE spokesperson Elisa Romano. “After months of fruitless negotiations, we had no alternative but to take this step.”

At the heart of the dispute are staff concerns over a proposed restructuring plan, which union leaders argue would eliminate up to 6,500 jobs nationwide and increase workloads for remaining employees. Bank management representatives, speaking through the Italian Banking Association, stated that the restructuring is necessary to adapt to changing market conditions and increased adoption of digital services by customers. However, unions insist the measures go too far and risk undermining service quality and worker well-being.

Industry analysts note that this is the largest coordinated strike in the Italian banking sector since 2015. “The scale of participation indicates deep dissatisfaction among employees,” said Marco Bellini, financial sector analyst at Capital Insight. “While banks have invested heavily in digital transformation, there has been less focus on managing the human impact of those changes.”

The effects of the strike have been felt most acutely in regions with a high density of bank branches, such as Lombardy and Emilia-Romagna. Some banks have issued statements reassuring customers that essential services, including ATM withdrawals and online account access, remain operational, though with potential delays in transaction processing.

Negotiations between union leaders and employer representatives resumed Tuesday afternoon, but no agreement had been reached at the time of writing. “We are ready to sit down at the table and find a solution that respects both the needs of the industry and the rights of employees,” Romano said. 

The union has warned that if talks do not yield progress, further strikes could follow in the coming weeks.
